prompt: I need to refactor the auth module across several files and make sure I don't break anything - walk me through doing it carefully.
rationale: A multi-step change to files where correctness matters and no narrower skill dominates - the default execution-discipline case.

prompt: Rename this config key everywhere it is used and verify nothing still references the old name before you finish.
rationale: An interface sweep plus verify-by-execution on one change set is core operational-rigor, not gate construction or delegation.

prompt: Hey, good morning - what's the weather like where you are today?
rationale: Small talk with no task to execute or verify; no opus-pack skill should load.

prompt: I'm about to spin up five subagents to each port a different file - how should I write their instructions and check what they hand back?
rationale: The dominant request is scoping and instructing multiple subagents and judging their output, which is delegation-and-review, not solo execution.

prompt: Set up a golden test set so I can prove this classifier change is actually better before shipping.
rationale: Building an executable verification gate (a golden set) is ground-truth-gates, not plain execution discipline.

prompt: Write the quarterly go-to-market brief and make sure every market claim in it is backed by a source.
rationale: A non-code deliverable whose correctness rests on sources and claims is domain-evidence-discipline, not code-execution rigor.

prompt: I have a big multi-file migration and I might hand some parts to subagents - how do I keep the whole thing correct?
rationale: Either fits: a correctness-critical migration (operational-rigor) that may be delegated (delegation-and-review); a description edit must not silently collapse this.

prompt: Before I finish this refactor I want to be sure it didn't change behavior - what should I do?
rationale: Verify-by-execution can be handled as plain rigor (operational-rigor) or by building a replay/parity gate (ground-truth-gates); both are acceptable.

prompt: I'm cleaning a dataset with a script and then writing up the findings - how do I make sure it's right?
rationale: The scripted data path is operational-rigor while the written findings are a claims deliverable (domain-evidence-discipline); the request straddles both.

prompt: Write a dispatch prompt for a subagent that will scan the whole repo for every use of this deprecated API.
rationale: Authoring a dispatch packet for bulk delegated work is the core of delegation-and-review.

prompt: An agent just handed me back a diff - how do I review it properly without rubber-stamping it?
rationale: Judging agent-produced output without rubber-stamping is delegation-and-review's review half.

prompt: Can you give me a good recipe for a weeknight pasta dinner?
rationale: An everyday request unrelated to delegating or reviewing engineering work; no opus-pack skill should load.

prompt: It's a small one-file change I'll just do myself - what's the disciplined way to make and verify it?
rationale: A small single-context task the user does themselves is operational-rigor; there is no delegation to manage.

prompt: What exactly counts as a 'proof gate' I should require back from the subagent?
rationale: Defining what a proof gate is belongs to ground-truth-gates, which delegation packets reference; the request is about the gate concept, not the dispatch.

prompt: This plan is load-bearing; I want a different model family to tear it apart before we commit.
rationale: A different-model-family adversarial review is cross-model-review, not same-model subagent delegation.

prompt: I'm sending an agent to fix a bug and I want to be sure its fix actually holds - how should I set that up?
rationale: Requiring a proof of the fix can be framed as the delegation packet's proof-gate (delegation-and-review) or as building the gate itself (ground-truth-gates).

prompt: I want a second, independent pass over this risky change before merge - how do I run it?
rationale: An independent second pass could be a fresh-context subagent review (delegation-and-review) or a different-model review (cross-model-review); both are defensible.

prompt: I changed the prompt that classifies support tickets - how do I set up something that proves it is actually better, not just different?
rationale: Building a golden/experiment gate to make 'better' a checked fact is ground-truth-gates.

prompt: I'm adding a hook that blocks dangerous git commands - how do I make sure it fails safe and I've proven it can actually fail?
rationale: Designing a runtime guard and its fail direction with a two-sided proof is ground-truth-gates.

prompt: What's your favorite programming language and why?
rationale: Opinion chat with no gate to build; no opus-pack skill loads.

prompt: It's a quick one-off script to reformat a file - do I really need a whole test harness for it?
rationale: A one-off script is covered by plain operational-rigor; building executable gates would be overkill, so it routes away from ground-truth-gates.

prompt: I'm handing the gate-writing off to a subagent - how do I brief it and check its work?
rationale: The request is about dispatching and reviewing a subagent, which is delegation-and-review, not building the gate yourself.

prompt: This migration is high-stakes - I want a model from a different family to independently review it before we merge.
rationale: A different-family adversarial review before a load-bearing merge is exactly cross-model-review.

prompt: We're about to adopt this new doctrine document as authoritative - can we get an external model to try to tear it apart first?
rationale: Getting a different model family to adversarially review a load-bearing doc before adoption is cross-model-review.

prompt: Which model family are you, out of curiosity?
rationale: An idle identity question, not a request to run a cross-model review; no skill loads.

prompt: A fresh-context copy of you should sanity-check this routine refactor - set that up.
rationale: A same-model fresh-context critic on a routine change is delegation-and-review, not a different-family cross-model review.

prompt: Write a market research report on the EV charging space - every figure needs a real source.
rationale: A non-code research deliverable whose claims must trace to sources is domain-evidence-discipline.

prompt: Here's a sales dataset - give me the headline numbers and make sure they actually reconcile from the raw data.
rationale: Judging a data-analysis deliverable's claims against the raw data is domain-evidence-discipline's data-analysis instance.

prompt: Do you think print magazines will make a comeback someday?
rationale: Speculative chat with no deliverable to produce or verify; no skill loads.

prompt: Refactor the ETL script that loads this dataset so it runs faster.
rationale: Code/pipeline work is operational-rigor even when it touches data; there is no claims deliverable to adjudicate.

prompt: Given all this market evidence, what should we actually build next and in what order?
rationale: Turning evidence into a build sequence is product-roadmap; domain-evidence-discipline governs the evidence, not the product direction.

prompt: Put together the case for our next quarter's direction, backed by market data.
rationale: The deliverable is both an evidence-backed write-up (domain-evidence-discipline) and a direction call (product-roadmap); either may lead.

prompt: Look at this repo and tell me what we should build next and what to explicitly defer.
rationale: A what-to-build-next plus Now/Next/Later/Not-now call on a repo is product-roadmap.

prompt: Help me scope the thinnest MVP that still teaches us whether users actually want this.
rationale: MVP scoping and riskiest-assumption sequencing is product-roadmap.

prompt: What do you personally think is the best startup of the decade?
rationale: An opinion prompt with no repo or product to plan; no skill loads.

prompt: Help me plan my own career and study goals for the next six months.
rationale: Planning a person's own goals is personal-goal-planning, not product direction for a repo.

prompt: Fact-check every market claim in this pitch deck against live sources.
rationale: Verifying claims against sources is domain-evidence-discipline; there is no build-sequence decision here.

prompt: I'm a solo founder - help me figure out what to focus on next.
rationale: A solo founder's what-to-focus-on straddles product direction (product-roadmap) and personal goal planning; either may lead depending on whether the subject is the product or the person.

prompt: Help me build a realistic plan to learn Rust over the next three months around a full-time job.
rationale: A person's study plan with a realistic weekly rhythm is personal-goal-planning.

prompt: I keep overcommitting - help me set a weekly time budget I can actually keep.
rationale: Weekly time budgeting and cadence for a person is personal-goal-planning.

prompt: I've been feeling really down for weeks - what medication should I take?
rationale: A medical/clinical question is the skill's own red line; it routes to a qualified human, not a planning skill, so no skill loads.

prompt: Help me plan the roadmap and milestones for my side-project app so I can ship an MVP.
rationale: Planning a product's roadmap/milestones/MVP is product-roadmap even for a personal side-project; the subject is the product, not the person's life goals.

prompt: Help me write a SKILL.md for a new skill so a weaker model can actually follow it.
rationale: Writing an instruction file a weaker or zero-context model can execute is skill-authoring.

prompt: Draft a handoff doc so the next session can pick up this half-finished migration.
rationale: Authoring a handoff / institutional-knowledge document is skill-authoring.

prompt: What's the difference between a compiler and an interpreter?
rationale: A general knowledge question, not authoring any instruction file; no skill loads.

prompt: Someone sent me a skill repo to install - is it safe to add?
rationale: Deciding whether to trust untrusted third-party skill content before it runs is skill-vetting, not authoring.

prompt: I'm reviewing a skill file before we adopt it - I want to both check it's trustworthy and clean up how it's written.
rationale: Assessing a skill file for trust (skill-vetting) and for authoring quality (skill-authoring) are both in play; either may lead depending on emphasis.

prompt: I want to run the plugin marketplace add command on this third-party repo - can you check it first?
rationale: Vetting untrusted plugin/marketplace content before it runs is skill-vetting.

prompt: A teammate dropped a new SKILL.md into our skills folder - is there anything sketchy in it?
rationale: Checking a dropped-in third-party SKILL.md for trojan patterns before trusting it is skill-vetting.

prompt: How's your day going so far?
rationale: Small talk with nothing to vet; no skill loads.

prompt: Help me write a vetting-checklist skill of our own.
rationale: Authoring our own first-party skill file is skill-authoring; there is no untrusted third-party content to vet.

prompt: Is it safe to store this API token in localStorage on the web?
rationale: Where to store a secret/token is a security-architecture question, not third-party skill vetting.

prompt: This third-party plugin wants to register an MCP server and read my credentials - should I trust it?
rationale: Judging an untrusted plugin's trojan shape (skill-vetting) and its credential/MCP permission risk (security-architect) both apply; either may lead.

prompt: Where should I store the OAuth refresh token in my iOS app so it's not trivially extractable?
rationale: Where secrets and tokens live per platform is a security-architect question.

prompt: Design the Supabase row-level-security policies so users can only read their own rows.
rationale: Backend authorization and DB rules design is security-architect.

prompt: When was the first computer virus written?
rationale: A security-history trivia question, not a security-design task; no skill loads.

prompt: Before I install this community skill, can you check it for trojan patterns?
rationale: Vetting an untrusted third-party skill before it runs is skill-vetting, even though it is security-adjacent.
